issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s right to recover possession for subletting that occurred under a repealed rent-control law survives repeal when that law made the subletting a ground for possession and required no prior termination notice.
material_facts: The tenancy contract did not prohibit subletting, but the rent-control law then in force absolutely prohibited it and entitled the landlord to recover possession on that ground.
The tenants sublet the premises while that law was in force.
That law was repealed and replaced by a law under which the subletting was not unlawful absent a contractual prohibition.
The landlord gave notice and brought the possession suit only after the repeal.
issues.conclusion: The landlord’s right to recover possession had accrued when the tenants sublet the premises under the former law, survived its repeal under section 51, provisos (1)(ii) and (2), of the Bombay Act, and could be enforced by a suit filed after repeal.
issues.legal_principle: A repeal saving clause preserves specific rights acquired or accrued from events that occurred under the repealed law, as well as proceedings or remedies to enforce them; it does not preserve a merely abstract right or a hope dependent on a further condition. If the former law required termination of the tenancy before a possession right accrued, that step would have to occur before repeal. Here it did not: the Saurashtra Rent Control Act, 1951, sections 13(1)(e) and 15, made subletting a ground for possession without requiring a prior notice terminating the tenancy, so the right accrued upon subletting and was preserved by section 51 of the Bombay Act. The Court relied on Hamilton Coll v. White, Abbott v. Minister of Lands, Director of Public Works v. Ho Po Sang, and Free Lanka Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Ranasinghe on the distinction between an accrued right and a mere expectation.

predicates.eviction_suit_after_repeal: A landlord brought a suit to recover possession after the law under which the alleged ground arose had been repealed.
predicates.subletting_under_prior_law: A tenant sublet the premises while the former law was in force.
predicates.prior_law_made_subletting_a_ground_for_p: The former law entitled the landlord to recover possession because the tenant sublet the premises.
predicates.prior_law_required_no_prior_termination_: The former law did not require the landlord to terminate the tenancy by notice before seeking possession on that ground.

issues.definition: When a tenant sublets premises under a former law that made subletting a ground for possession without requiring prior termination notice, a landlord may enforce that possession right in a suit brought after the law is repealed.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord need not give a notice under the Transfer of Property Act to terminate a tenancy on the ground of subletting when the tenancy contract does not prohibit subletting and the applicable rent-control law independently makes subletting a ground for possession.
material_facts: The tenancy contract contained no prohibition against subletting.
The former rent-control law prohibited subletting independently of the contract and provided a ground for recovering possession on that basis.
The landlord relied on the statutory subletting ground to seek possession.
issues.conclusion: No notice under the Transfer of Property Act was necessary to terminate the tenancy on the ground of subletting.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 111 of the Transfer of Property Act, forfeiture for breach depends on a breach of a condition of the tenancy contract that entails forfeiture. Subletting is not such a breach when the contract does not prohibit it, and the Transfer of Property Act therefore does not allow the landlord to terminate the tenancy on that ground by notice. The statutory right to possession in this case arose instead under sections 13(1)(e) and 15 of the Saurashtra Rent Control Act, 1951, which prohibited subletting independently of the contract and did not require prior notice terminating the tenancy.

predicates.eviction_case_based_on_subletting: A landlord sought possession in an eviction proceeding on the ground that the tenant had sublet the premises.
predicates.tenancy_contract_did_not_prohibit_sublet: The tenancy contract did not bar the tenant from subletting the premises.
predicates.rent_law_independently_made_subletting_a: The applicable rent-control law independently prohibited subletting and made it a ground for possession.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks possession because of subletting that the contract permits but the rent-control law independently prohibits, no Transfer of Property Act notice is required to terminate the tenancy on that ground.
